name: Pontine nuclei
function: Relay station of the cortico-ponto-cerebellar system: cortical association and motor fibers synapse on pontine gray neurons, whose axons cross the midline as transverse pontocerebellar fibers and reach the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere through the middle cerebellar peduncle. This massive relay lets the cerebral cortex enlist the cerebellum in the planning and coordination of skilled movement.

afferent: Corticopontine fibers (frontopontine and temporoparietooccipitopontine bundles, tract-corticopontine)
efferent: Pontocerebellar fibers crossing to the contralateral cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle (tract-mcp)

bloodSupply: Basilar artery paramedian and short circumferential perforators

clinical.findings: Basis pontis infarction (including the pontine relay gray) abolishes nearly all voluntary movement except vertical eye movements and blinking, while the dorsal tegmentum and consciousness are spared.
Osmotic stress demyelinates the central basis pontis, damaging the pontine gray and the fiber systems threading through it, and producing spastic quadriparesis with pseudobulbar palsy.
clinical.note: Classically follows over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia.

contextNote: Context silhouette of the basis-pontis relay gray for the 3D envelope and sagittal/coronal plates; the individual longitudinal tracts threading through the basis are separate records (tract-corticospinal-lateral, tract-corticobulbar, tract-corticopontine in tracts.json).
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes, RadioGraphics 2019 (doi 10.1148/rg.2019180126)

name: Longitudinal and transverse pontine fibers
function: Composite fiber systems of the basis pontis: the longitudinal fasciculi carry corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine axons from the crus cerebri down to the medulla, while the transverse fibers arise from the pontine nuclei, decussate, and collect laterally as the middle cerebellar peduncle.

afferent: Corticofugal bundles from the crus cerebri (tract-corticospinal-lateral, tract-corticobulbar, tract-corticopontine)
efferent: Pontocerebellar fibers forming the middle cerebellar peduncle (tract-mcp)

clinical.findings: Interruption of the longitudinal fibers in the ventral pons disconnects the motor cortex from all spinal and cranial motor nuclei below, sparing only the oculomotor pathways in the tegmentum.

A small paramedian lacunar infarct confined to the basis pontis destroys descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres together with the transverse pontocerebellar fibres, so the patient shows a clumsy, slow hand with mild weakness of the same limbs and dysarthria — plus gait ataxia disproportionate to the weakness. Larger lesions produce the full locked-in picture.
clinical.note: The transverse fibres decussate here and gather as the middle cerebellar peduncle, so a unilateral basis lesion also de-afferents the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere and can add crossed cerebellar ataxia.

contextNote: Context record for the basis-pontis fiber feltwork; the named descending pathways are tracked individually in tracts.json and are tagged separately on transverse plates.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Trigeminal motor nucleus (CN V)
function: Lower motor neurons innervating the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) plus tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric through the motor root of CN V (portio minor). It executes the jaw-jerk (masseteric) reflex and receives predominantly bilateral corticobulbar input, so supranuclear lesions cause only mild contralateral jaw weakness.

afferent: Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus and tract (jaw-closure proprioception for the jaw-jerk reflex)
Corticobulbar fibers (bilateral)
Reticular formation pattern generators for chewing
efferent: Motor root of CN V (portio minor) to the muscles of mastication and tensor muscles

bloodSupply: Basilar paramedian perforators; superior cerebellar artery branches at the rostral pole

clinical.findings: Wasting and weakness of the ipsilateral masticatory muscles; on opening, the jaw deviates toward the weak side (unopposed lateral pterygoid of the normal side), and the jaw jerk is abolished.
clinical.vascular: Short circumferential branches of the basilar artery (superior cerebellar artery branches at the rostral pole)
clinical.note: In striking contrast, UMN (corticobulbar) lesions weaken the jaw only slightly because the nucleus is bilaterally innervated.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Patten, Neurological Differential Diagnosis, 2nd ed., brainstem level plates

name: Principal sensory trigeminal nucleus
function: Second-order relay of the trigeminal system for large-fiber discriminative touch, pressure and periodontal mechanoreception: entering portio-major afferents of CN V terminate here, and the neurons project chiefly through the decussating ventral trigeminothalamic (trigeminal lemniscus) tract to the contralateral ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM), with a smaller ipsilateral dorsal trigeminothalamic stream.

afferent: Mechanoreceptive afferents of the CN V sensory root (portio major) from face, oral cavity and tooth pulp
efferent: Ventral trigeminothalamic tract (tract-trigeminothalamic-ventral) to contralateral VPM
Dorsal trigeminothalamic tract (tract-trigeminothalamic-dorsal), ipsilateral

bloodSupply: Short circumferential branches of the basilar artery; AICA territory caudally, SCA rostrally

clinical.findings: Lateral pontine lesions involving the nucleus blunt ipsilateral discriminative touch over the face while pain-temperature (spinal trigeminal complex) is spared or affected separately, helping localize the lesion to the mid-pons.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Snell, Clinical Neuroanatomy, brainstem and cranial nerves chapters

name: Abducens nucleus (CN VI)
function: Contains two populations: lower motor neurons driving the ipsilateral lateral rectus (abduction of that eye), and internuclear neurons whose axons cross immediately, ascend in the contralateral medial longitudinal fasciculus, and excite medial-rectus motoneurons of the oculomotor complex — yoking both eyes into conjugate horizontal gaze. The nucleus therefore functions as the final common command for looking toward its own side.

afferent: Excitatory burst neurons of the ipsilateral PPRF (nuc-pprf)
Vestibular nuclei via the MLF (vestibulo-ocular reflex)
Corticobulbar gaze fibers
efferent: CN VI fibers to the ipsilateral lateral rectus
Internuclear axons crossing to ascend in the contralateral MLF toward nuc-oculomotor

bloodSupply: Basilar artery paramedian perforators at the pontomedullary junction

clinical.findings: A nuclear CN VI lesion paralyses gaze toward the lesion: the ipsilateral eye cannot abduct AND the contralateral eye cannot adduct past the midline, because the internuclear neurons are destroyed together with the motor neurons.
clinical.note: This distinguishes a nuclear lesion (gaze palsy) from a fascicular or peripheral CN VI lesion (isolated failure of abduction with diplopia).

clinical.syndrome: Horizontal diplopia from fascicular CN VI injury
clinical.findings: If only the exiting motor fibers are damaged, the ipsilateral eye fails to abduct and images separate worst at distance; common in Millard-Gubler and basal pontine lesions.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes, RadioGraphics 2019 (doi 10.1148/rg.2019180126)

name: Facial nucleus (CN VII)
function: Lower motor neurons for all muscles of facial expression plus stapedius, stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric. Axons arc dorsomedially around the abducens nucleus (the internal genu, producing the facial colliculus) before turning ventrolaterally to exit. Corticobulbar input to the upper-face division is bilateral, whereas the lower-face division is driven mainly by the contralateral cortex — the anatomical basis of the central versus peripheral facial palsy patterns.

afferent: Corticobulbar fibers (bilateral for the upper face, contralateral-dominant for the lower face)
Reflex afferents from the spinal trigeminal complex (corneal blink) and from the superior olivary complex (stapedial reflex)
efferent: CN VII motor root to the muscles of facial expression and stapedius

clinical.findings: Paralysis of the entire ipsilateral hemiface including the forehead: the eye will not close, tears pool, food collects in the buccal vestibule and the smile flattens; hyperacusis may appear if stapedius fibers are involved. Nuclear or fascicular lesions combine this with other pontine deficits (Millard-Gubler).
Contralateral weakness confined to the lower face with forehead sparing, produced by lesions of the corticobulbar fibers above the nucleus (cortex, internal capsule, cerebral peduncle).
clinical.note: Forehead sparing reflects the bilateral cortical innervation of the upper-division motoneurons.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Patten, Neurological Differential Diagnosis, 2nd ed., facial palsy localization sections

name: Superior salivatory nucleus
function: Parasympathetic preganglionic column of CN VII: its fibers travel with the nervus intermedius, then via the greater petrosal nerve to the pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal gland and nasal-palatal mucosa) and via the chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion (submandibular and sublingual glands), driving tear production and salivation.

afferent: Hypothalamic and olfactory (visceral emotional) inputs modulating lacrimation and salivation
efferent: Nervus intermedius — greater petrosal nerve to the pterygopalatine ganglion; chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion

clinical.syndrome: Ipsilateral dry eye and reduced salivation
clinical.findings: Pontine or proximal CN VII lesions involving the nucleus or nervus intermedius reduce lacrimation and submandibular-sublingual salivation; the same fibers are affected in Bell palsy, explaining dry eye and altered taste together.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Nucleus solitarius (rostral gustatory part)
function: Rostral (gustatory) pole of the solitary nuclear complex reaching the caudal pons: the first central synapse for taste afferents of CN VII (chorda tympani, greater petrosal), CN IX and CN X. Output rises in the central tegmental tract to the parabrachial nuclei and, via thalamic relay in VPM, to the insular gustatory cortex.

afferent: Taste-bud primary afferents via CN VII, CN IX and CN X
efferent: Central tegmental tract (tract-central-tegmental) to parabrachial nuclei and VPM
Hypothalamic and amygdaloid viscerosensory projections

bloodSupply: Basilar short circumferential branches; AICA at the pontomedullary junction

clinical.findings: Rare in isolated form; loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior two-thirds of the tongue accompanies pontine lesions of the solitary complex or its central tegmental output.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Superior vestibular nucleus
function: Rostral-most vestibular nucleus, lying at the lateral angle of the fourth-ventricle floor near the cerebellar peduncles: integrates semicircular-canal signals and feeds vestibulo-ocular reflex pathways through the MLF to the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nuclei, and exchanges fibers with the vestibulocerebellum.

afferent: Superior and lateral semicircular canal afferents of CN VIII
Flocculonodular (vestibulocerebellar) Purkinje fibers
efferent: Ascending MLF fibers to the oculomotor nuclei (VOR)
Vestibulocerebellar fibers via the inferior cerebellar peduncle (tract-icp)

clinical.findings: Unilateral involvement produces vertigo with nystagmus and past-pointing as part of AICA or lateral pontine syndromes.

clinical.syndrome: Skew deviation and the ocular tilt reaction (otolith pathway)
clinical.findings: Utricular signals relayed through the superior vestibular nucleus are distributed by the MLF to the ocular motor nuclei and to the interstitial nucleus of Cajal; when they become asymmetric — a superior vestibular nerve or nucleus lesion, or a brainstem tegmental lesion — the brain misjudges 'down' and produces an ocular tilt reaction of head tilt, skew deviation (one eye higher than the other) and conjugate ocular torsion. The direction of the tilt indicates the side of the imbalanced utricular input.
clinical.note: Skew deviation is a graviceptive (otolith) sign, not a nerve palsy: ductions and versions are full, and the vertical diplopia is commonly dissociated from the degree of vertigo.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, vestibular system section

name: Medial vestibular nucleus
function: The longest vestibular nucleus, extending from the open medulla into the mid-pons: principal source of the medial vestibulospinal tract and of the MLF vestibulo-ocular fibers that stabilize gaze during head movement; also relays to the reticular formation (motion-sickness pathways) and the cerebellum.

afferent: CN VIII canal and macular afferents
Vestibulocerebellar Purkinje fibers
efferent: Medial vestibulospinal tract (tract-medial-vestibulospinal)
Bilateral MLF projections to the extraocular motor nuclei
Reticular formation and tract-icp projections

clinical.findings: Lesions impair the vestibulo-ocular reflex, producing oscillopsia, gaze-evoked nystagmus and impaired smooth pursuit-vestibular cooperation in lateral pontomedullary strokes.

clinical.syndrome: Lateropulsion (ipsilateral trunk push) in lateral medullary and vestibular lesions
clinical.findings: The medial vestibular nucleus is the source of the medial vestibulospinal tract and of the MLF vestibulo-ocular fibres, so its involvement — classically in a Wallenberg infarct — produces lateropulsion: the patient actively pushes the trunk and falls toward the side of the lesion, with the head and eyes deviated the same way, and the symptom may outlast the vertigo and nystagmus by weeks.
clinical.vascular: PICA / vertebral (dorsolateral medulla); AICA at the pontine level
clinical.note: Distinguishing lateropulsion (vestibulospinal, toward the lesion) from cerebellar past-pointing (limb, ipsilateral, with dysmetria) is a classic bedside discriminator.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Lateral vestibular nucleus
function: Deiters nucleus: gives origin to the ipsilateral lateral vestibulospinal tract, which facilitates extensor (antigravity) muscle tone of the limbs and trunk for postural support; governed by inhibitory Purkinje input from the vestibulocerebellar vermis, so loss of cerebellar restraint yields excessive extensor tone.

afferent: CN VIII otolith (utricular) afferents
Inhibitory Purkinje fibers of the vestibulocerebellum
efferent: Lateral vestibulospinal tract (tract-lateral-vestibulospinal)
Ascending vestibular projections for eye-head coordination

clinical.findings: Acute unilateral involvement contributes to ipsilateral past-pointing and postural instability (falling toward the lesion); decerebrate extensor rigidity reflects release of the lateral vestibulospinal system from cerebellar control.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, vestibular system section

name: Inferior vestibular nucleus
function: Caudalmost, longitudinally oriented vestibular nucleus descending toward the upper cervical cord: integrates vestibular input with spinocerebellar afferents and projects through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the vestibulocerebellum and to the reticular formation for vestibulo-spinal tuning.

afferent: CN VIII vestibular afferents
Spinocerebellar and spinal collaterals
efferent: Vestibulocerebellar fibers via tract-icp
Descending vestibulospinal and reticular connections

clinical.findings: The inferior (descending) vestibular nucleus processes vertical-canal and otolith signals and is the caudalmost link between the vestibular nerve and the vestibulocerebellum; lesions at the caudal medulla or craniocervical junction — a dorsal PICA-territory infarct, a small cerebellar haemorrhage or a Chiari malformation — are associated with vertical (typically downbeat) or direction-changing positional nystagmus, postural instability with falls, and dysequilibrium that outlasts the acute vertigo.
clinical.note: Hearing is usually preserved: the cochlear nuclei and nerve root lie rostral to this nucleus, which is why a 'vestibular' medullary infarct can present exactly like vestibular neuritis.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Ventral cochlear nucleus
function: First central relay of hearing: spiral-ganglion axons of the cochlear division of CN VIII terminate on its bushy and multipolar cells, which preserve timing and intensity coding and launch the binaural pathway by sending axons through the trapezoid body to the contralateral superior olivary complex and into the lateral lemniscus of both sides.

afferent: Auditory (cochlear) nerve fibers from the spiral ganglion, tonotopically arranged
efferent: Trapezoid body (tract-trapezoid-body)
Superior olivary complex (nuc-superior-olivary)
Contralateral lateral lemniscus (tract-lateral-lemniscus)

clinical.findings: Destruction of the cochlear nuclei or the entering CN VIII fibers abolishes ipsilateral hearing (there is no bilateral backup at this first relay); classically produced by AICA infarction or cerebellopontine-angle tumors.
clinical.vascular: Short circumferential branches of the basilar artery (AICA territory for the caudal part of the nucleus)
clinical.note: Beyond the cochlear nuclei, auditory information is bilaterally represented, so central lesions cause only subtle hearing loss.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Nolte, The Human Brain, auditory system chapter

name: Dorsal cochlear nucleus
function: Laminated nucleus forming the acoustic tubercle on the dorsolateral brainstem surface over the inferior cerebellar peduncle: its principal (fusiform) cells integrate auditory input with somatosensory and vestibular modulation and project directly into the contralateral lateral lemniscus, contributing to spectral-shape cues used for vertical-plane sound localization.

afferent: Auditory nerve afferents across the tonotopic range (the nucleus maps high frequencies dorsally)
Somatosensory and vestibular modulatory inputs
efferent: Contralateral lateral lemniscus (tract-lateral-lemniscus) via the acoustic striae

clinical.syndrome: Ipsilateral sensorineural deafness with tinnitus (cerebellopontine angle lesion)
clinical.findings: Compression or infarction of the dorsal cochlear nucleus at the cerebellopontine angle — the usual site of a vestibular schwannoma, an AICA-territory infarct or an epidermoid — removes hearing and adds tinnitus on that side, usually with vertigo and facial numbness from the neighbouring structures. Because the auditory pathway decussates at the trapezoid body and is bilateral from the cochlear nuclei onwards, lesions above this level never cause unilateral deafness.
clinical.note: Its surface bulge is the acoustic tubercle over the inferior cerebellar peduncle; the nucleus is also a site of somatosensory-auditory convergence implicated in tinnitus generation.

refs: Nolte, The Human Brain, auditory system chapter
Duke Neurobiology, Brainstem Sectional Anatomy Lab (brain.oit.duke.edu/lab03)

name: Superior olivary complex
function: First site of binaural convergence in the auditory pathway: the medial superior olive computes interaural time differences and the lateral superior olive interaural intensity differences, providing the neural map of horizontal sound direction; the complex also houses medial olivocochlear neurons whose efferent fibers tune the organ of Corti via the vestibulocochlear anastomosis.

afferent: Ventral cochlear nucleus neurons via the trapezoid body (tract-trapezoid-body) and medial nucleus of the trapezoid body
efferent: Lateral lemniscus (tract-lateral-lemniscus) to the inferior colliculus
Olivocochlear efferent bundle back to the cochlea

clinical.syndrome: Loss of binaural sound localization (impaired interaural processing)
clinical.findings: The complex is the brain's first binaural comparator, so a lesion that removes it — typically a small basilar or AICA-territory pontine infarct — leaves pure-tone thresholds relatively preserved while destroying the ability to judge which side a sound comes from and degrading speech understanding against background noise; the deficit is easily missed because routine audiometry is normal.
clinical.note: The same complex gives rise to the medial olivocochlear bundle, so its damage also removes efferent control of the cochlea (protection from loud sound and the 'anti-masking' reflex).

refs: Nolte, The Human Brain, auditory system chapter
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"

name: Trapezoid body
synonyms: auditory decussation of the caudal pons
function: Horizontal band of decussating auditory fibers sweeping across the ventral tegmentum of the caudal pons: axons of ventral cochlear nucleus neurons cross here to reach the contralateral superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus, guaranteeing that both inferior colliculi (and both auditory cortices) respond to either ear.

afferent: Ventral cochlear nucleus (nuc-cochlear-ventral) axons
efferent: Superior olivary complex (nuc-superior-olivary) and lateral lemniscus (tract-lateral-lemniscus), contralateral

bloodSupply: Basilar paramedian and short circumferential perforators

clinical.syndrome: Bilateral representation of each ear (auditory decussation)
clinical.findings: The trapezoid body is the first decussation of the auditory system: section of it, or of the ventral cochlear nucleus output that feeds it, removes the crossed contribution of one ear to the opposite lateral lemniscus. Clinically this is expressed as part of a ventral caudal pontine infarct, where the auditory finding is muffled hearing and impaired sound localization rather than an isolated deafness, because the uncrossed projection from each cochlear nucleus survives.
clinical.vascular: Basilar paramedian and short circumferential perforators
clinical.note: This decussation is why each inferior colliculus and each auditory cortex is driven by both ears — and why a brainstem lesion almost never causes unilateral deafness.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Nolte, The Human Brain, auditory system chapter

name: Lateral lemniscus
function: Tonotopically organized ascending auditory bundle running in the subpial lateral tegmentum beside the middle cerebellar peduncle: it carries binaural information from the cochlear nuclei and superior olivary complex (via its interspersed lemniscal nuclei) rostrally to terminate in the inferior colliculus of the midbrain.

afferent: Cochlear nuclei (nuc-cochlear-ventral, nuc-cochlear-dorsal) and superior olivary complex (nuc-superior-olivary)
efferent: Inferior colliculus (nuc-inferior-colliculus), thence the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus

bloodSupply: Short circumferential branches of the basilar artery; SCA rostrally

clinical.syndrome: Auditory component of the lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome
clinical.findings: The lateral lemniscus lies in the subpial lateral tegmentum beside the middle cerebellar peduncle, exactly where an AICA infarct lands: patients then report tinnitus and reduced hearing on that side, although the damage that produces the deafness is at the cochlear nuclei and nerve root rather than in the lemniscus itself. An isolated lemniscal lesion barely changes pure-tone thresholds because each lemniscus already carries information from both ears (the ventral cochlear nuclei project bilaterally through the trapezoid body); the typical residual is difficulty localizing sound and understanding speech in noise.
clinical.note: Teaching point for localization: unilateral deafness is never central — it points to the cochlea, the auditory nerve or the cochlear nuclei, not to this bundle.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Nolte, The Human Brain, auditory system chapter

name: Middle cerebellar peduncle
function: The largest fiber system of the brainstem: the lateral continuation of the transverse pontocerebellar fibers, carrying crossed cortico-ponto-cerebellar information from each pontine gray into the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere; it is strictly an afferent peduncle of the cerebellum and dominates the lateral aspect of every mid- and upper-pontine section.

afferent: Pontine nuclei (ctx-pontine-nuclei) after hemidecussation of pontocerebellar fibers
efferent: Contralateral cerebellar hemisphere cortex (ctx-cerebellum)

bloodSupply: AICA (caudal) and SCA (rostral) short circumferential branches of the basilar artery

clinical.findings: Unilateral MCP damage (infarct, demyelination, pontine tumors) produces severe ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia with dysmetria, because the peduncle feeds the ipsilateral (already double-crossed) cerebellar hemisphere.
T2 hyperintensity and atrophy of the MCP is a classic MRI sign in spinocerebellar ataxias, fragile-X tremor-ataxia syndrome and Wilson disease.
clinical.note: The sign localizes to degeneration of pontocerebellar fibers rather than to a vascular event.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes, RadioGraphics 2019 (doi 10.1148/rg.2019180126)

name: Locus coeruleus
function: The principal noradrenergic nucleus of the brain: about half of all brain norepinephrine arises here, and its axons ramify through virtually the entire neuraxis (neocortex, hippocampus, thalamus, cerebellum and spinal cord). Phasic LC firing sharpens attention to salient stimuli and gates cortical plasticity; tonic firing sets global arousal and helps orchestrate the sleep-wake cycle, stress responses and descending pain modulation. Neuromelanin pigment gives the fresh nucleus its characteristic blue-black color.

afferent: Nucleus paragigantocellularis of the medullary reticular formation (autonomic drive)
Periaqueductal gray (pain/stress)
Hypothalamus (paraventricular nucleus)
Prepositus hypoglossi and solitary nucleus
efferent: Diffuse noradrenergic projections to neocortex, hippocampus, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum and spinal cord (ascending dorsal noradrenergic bundle)

bloodSupply: Basilar (rostral pontine) paramedian and short circumferential perforators, at the SCA/AICA boundary

clinical.findings: Noradrenergic denervation blunts vigilance, degrades sleep architecture and contributes to cognitive slowing; LC neurons degenerate early in Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease, and alpha-2 agonists/antagonists manipulate LC tone pharmacologically.
clinical.note: Because the LC is tiny and tightly paired to the fourth-ventricle floor, focal symptomatic infarcts are rare; dysfunction is mostly degenerative or pharmacologic.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, reticular formation and monoamines section

name: Pontine reticular formation (oral and caudal nuclei)
function: Core of the pontine tegmentum spanning the oral and caudal pontine reticular nuclei: contributes to ascending reticular activating (arousal) systems through the intralaminar thalamic nuclei, houses pontine generators of postural tone and of REM sleep, and gives origin to the pontine (medial) reticulospinal tract that facilitates antigravity extensor tone and gait-related posture.

afferent: Spinoreticular tract (tract-spinoreticular)
Sensorimotor cortex (corticoreticular fibers)
Cerebellar fastigial output
Collaterals of ascending sensory lemnisci
efferent: Pontine reticulospinal tract (tract-reticulospinal)
Intralaminar and midline thalamic nuclei (ascending arousal)
Central tegmental tract projections
Cranial nerve motor pattern-generator circuits

bloodSupply: Basilar paramedian perforators (tegmental branches); SCA branches rostrally

clinical.findings: Bilateral paramedian damage of the upper brainstem reticular core (basilar tip occlusion) abolishes arousal while the cortex itself is structurally spared — the classic brainstem (ascending reticular activating system) basis of coma.
Lesions of the pontine reticulospinal output bias antigravity tone; combined with PPRF damage this underlies the gaze-posture findings of dorsal pontine syndromes (Foville).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Fix, High-Yield Neuroanatomy, reticular formation section

name: Paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)
function: The horizontal conjugate gaze center: excitatory burst neurons here command ipsilateral saccades by driving the immediately adjacent abducens nucleus, whose motor neurons turn the ipsilateral eye out and whose internuclear neurons (crossing via the MLF) turn the contralateral eye in. Omnipause neurons within the PPRF gate burst onset; the frontal eye field and superior colliculus trigger it.

afferent: Frontal eye field (corticoreticular saccade command)
Superior colliculus (nuc-superior-colliculus)
Cerebellar vermis and fastigial calibration
Vestibular nuclei (slow-phase VOR drive)
efferent: Ipsilateral abducens nucleus (nuc-abducens) — motor and internuclear arms of the conjugate command
Inhibitory burst projections to the contralateral PPRF

clinical.findings: A unilateral PPRF lesion abolishes rapid conjugate gaze toward the lesion; the eyes rest deviated away, and the intact contralateral PPRF drives gaze in the opposite direction. Conjugacy is preserved, so diplopia is absent.
clinical.note: Doll's-eye (oculocephalic) or cold-caloric testing may still move the eyes because the vestibulo-ocular reflex reaches the abducens nucleus directly, bypassing the PPRF.

clinical.findings: Combined PPRF/abducens and ipsilateral MLF lesions leave only one residual eye movement — contralateral abduction — producing the one-and-a-half syndrome of the dorsal pons.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem II: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply"
Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes, RadioGraphics 2019 (doi 10.1148/rg.2019180126)

name: Trigeminal nerve (CN V) exit
function: The large sensory root (portio major) and the smaller medial motor root of CN V emerge together from the mid-lateral pons, crossing the prepontine cistern to the trigeminal (gasserian) ganglion in Meckel cave; the root carries all facial and cranial somatosensory afferents and, in its motor root, the fibers to the muscles of mastication.

clinical.findings: Root-zone lesions (CPA tumors, AICA aneurysms, demyelination) combine ipsilateral facial sensory loss with masseter weakness; vascular root compression at the entry zone underlies classic trigeminal neuralgia.
clinical.note: The root entry zone is the lateral benchmark of the midpontine level (lvl-pons-middle).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Abducens nerve (CN VI) exit
synonyms: CN VI root at pontomedullary junction
function: CN VI rootlets emerge ventromedially at the pontomedullary junction, between the pyramid and the middle cerebellar peduncle, then run the longest cisternal subarachnoid course in the posterior fossa, up the clival dura to Dorello's canal before entering the cavernous sinus and orbit.

clinical.findings: Horizontal diplopia worst at distance with failure of ipsilateral abduction; because of the long cisternal course, CN VI palsy is the classic false-localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure (stretching against the petrous ridge).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Facial nerve (CN VII) exit
synonyms: CN VII/VIII root at cerebellopontine angle
function: The facial nerve (motor root plus the nervus intermedius carrying taste and parasympathetic fibers) leaves the pontomedullary junction at the cerebellopontine angle, crosses the CPA cistern and enters the internal acoustic meatus alongside CN VIII.

clinical.findings: CPA masses (vestibular schwannoma, meningioma) or AICA infarcts compress/infarct CN VII at the exit zone, producing complete ipsilateral LMN facial weakness often with hearing loss and diminished corneal reflex.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) exit
function: The vestibulocochlear nerve crosses the cerebellopontine angle just behind the facial nerve and enters the internal acoustic meatus, carrying auditory afferents from the spiral ganglion and vestibular afferents from the vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion to the cochlear and vestibular nuclei at the pontomedullary junction.

clinical.findings: Progressive unilateral tinnitus and sensorineural hearing loss with vertigo and imbalance — the hallmark of vestibular schwannoma; sudden equivalents occur with AICA infarction.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Facial colliculus
synonyms: dorsal pontine bulge over abducens nucleus
function: The rounded bulge in the floor of the fourth ventricle over the abducens nucleus, produced by the internal genu of CN VII fibers sweeping dorsomedially around the nucleus before turning ventrally to exit; a landmark of the caudal pontine floor together with the neighboring median eminence and striae medullares.

clinical.findings: A lesion at the facial colliculus damages the abducens nucleus and the looping facial fibers together — ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy plus complete LMN facial paralysis (Foville syndrome), with loss of the ipsilateral blink.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. "Brainstem I: Surface Anatomy and Cross-Sectional Anatomy"

name: Pons (context surface)
function: Renderable silhouette of the whole pons as one block: the massively expanded basis pontis coursing ventrally to the middle cerebellar peduncles laterally, the pontine tegmentum dorsally with the fourth-ventricle floor, the facial colliculus and the trigeminal, facial and vestibulocochlear root exits on its surface. It exists so the pons is a single named, selectable body in the 3D scene, not because it is a nucleus; its internal content belongs to the pontine nucleus, tract and surface records.
